The Dataset

Alex · Ben · Gina · Linda · Margot · Otto
Topics: ethics, sponsorship transparency, audience relationships
Source: Renata Gonçalves Curty (UCSB), zenodo.org/records/18604273

All four methods use this same dataset. Having a shared dataset lets us compare what each method surfaces and what it misses.

title: Computational Approaches to Text Analysis
text:
What Is Software-Assisted QDA?
Structures what researchers have always done: read closely, annotate, and organize meaning.

Core functions:

Code: assign labels to passages
Memo: write interpretive notes
Query: search across codes and documents
Visualize: co-occurrence maps, frequency charts



The software does not find themes. It helps you track and retrieve the themes you identify.

Emphasize that QDA software is a tool for organizing human interpretation, not automating it. The analyst still makes every decision.

title: Computational Approaches to Text Analysis
text:
AI-Assisted Coding
AI can suggest codes, summarize passages, and group themes.

Best practice:

Structure prompts incrementally, one task at a time
Review every AI suggestion before accepting it
Document your prompts and model used
De-identify data before sending to any cloud model
Prefer local models for sensitive transcripts


The key tension is between efficiency and interpretive control. AI can speed up initial coding but introduces the risk of accepting suggestions without critical review.

Pre-Processing Steps
Before counting, text must be cleaned:

Tokenizing: split text into individual words
Normalizing: lowercase, remove punctuation
Filtering stop words: remove “the”, “and”, “is”
Lemmatizing: “promoting”, “promotes”, “promoted” → “promote”


These choices directly shape what the analysis surfaces.

title: Computational Approaches to Text Analysis
text:
What Is Sentiment Analysis?
Assigns a numerical score: positive, negative, or neutral.

VADER works from a lexicon of pre-scored words. Designed for short, informal social media text.



Score
Meaning




positive
Proportion of tokens with positive valence


negative
Proportion of tokens with negative valence


compound
−1.0 (most negative) to +1.0 (most positive)





Compound ≥ +0.05 = positive · ≤ −0.05 = negative · between = neutral

title: Computational Approaches to Text Analysis
text:
The Results

48 of 50 paragraphs score as positive


Compound scores cluster between +0.70 and +0.98
All six speakers have median scores above +0.75

title: Computational Approaches to Text Analysis
text:
What Does This Mean?
VADER reads honest, trust, values, responsible as positive.
But interview responses use these words to frame complex situations.

The tool cannot distinguish between:

“I believe in transparency” (conviction)
“I always say I believe in transparency” (performative)
“I believe in transparency, but sometimes it’s difficult” (with reservation)



The genre shapes the signal.

This is the key teaching moment for sentiment analysis. The near-uniform positive result is not about the speakers’ sincerity — it reflects the interview genre, where professional self-presentation calls for positive framing.

title: Computational Approaches to Text Analysis
text:
What the Scores Do Reveal
Even within a uniformly positive distribution:

Ben-003 scores negative — he is describing other influencers’ unethical behavior
Speakers with lower averages (Ben, Gina) use more hedged language
Box plot width shows tone consistency within each speaker


Full results: 3 · Sentiment Analysis

title: Computational Approaches to Text Analysis
text:
What Is Topic Modeling?
Groups documents by shared patterns — without reading each one individually.



Classical (LDA, NMF)
Groups by shared words

Neural (BERTopic)
Groups by shared meaning, even with different words



Trade-off: neural groupings are based on learned vector representations, so the reasoning behind a cluster is less directly readable from the output.

title: Computational Approaches to Text Analysis
text:
The Five-Step Pipeline

Embed: nomic-embed-text converts each paragraph to 768 numbers
Reduce: UMAP compresses 768 dimensions to 5
Cluster: HDBSCAN finds dense neighborhoods — no forced equal-sized groups
Extract words: c-TF-IDF finds distinctive words per cluster
Label: llama3.1 writes a human-readable topic name


Walk through each step slowly. The key conceptual jump is from text to numbers (embedding) — everything else flows from that.

title: What Is Topic Modeling?
text:
The Data You Will Analyze
The dataset contains 50 interview paragraphs drawn from transcripts with six digital influencers: Alex, Ben, Gina, Linda, Margot, and Otto. Each person describes their approach to brand partnerships, audience relationships, and ethical responsibilities in their own words. Each paragraph is treated as one document.



Column
What it contains




interview_id
A unique ID for each paragraph (e.g., ALEX-003)


interviewee
The speaker’s first name


paragraph_num
The paragraph’s position within that interview


text
The full text of the paragraph

title: What Is Topic Modeling?
text:
What Is Topic Modeling?
Topic modeling finds structure in a collection of texts without reading each one individually. It groups documents that share similar patterns, either by shared words (classical methods) or by shared meaning (neural methods like the one used here).
This project uses BERTopic, a neural topic modeling framework. The key difference from older approaches is in what “similar” means:

Classical topic modeling (e.g., LDA, NMF) groups documents that share distinctive words
Neural topic modeling (BERTopic) groups documents that share meaning, even if they use different words

Both are valid approaches. The neural approach is better at capturing paraphrase and implication. The trade-off is that the groupings are based on learned vector representations rather than word counts, so the reasoning behind a cluster is less directly readable from the output.

title: What Is Topic Modeling?
text:
The Five-Step Pipeline
The script runs these steps in sequence:
Step 1: Embed each paragraph. nomic-embed-text (a local language model running through Ollama) reads each paragraph and converts it into a list of 768 numbers. These numbers represent the paragraph’s meaning as a position in a high-dimensional space. Paragraphs that discuss similar ideas end up close together; paragraphs about different ideas end up far apart.
Step 2: Reduce dimensions with UMAP. 768 dimensions are hard to cluster. UMAP compresses the positions down to 5 dimensions while preserving the neighborhood structure. Paragraphs that were close in 768 dimensions stay close in 5.
Step 3: Cluster with HDBSCAN. HDBSCAN finds dense neighborhoods in the 5-dimensional space and calls each neighborhood a topic. Unlike algorithms that force equal-sized groups, HDBSCAN follows the actual density of the data. Paragraphs that do not belong to any dense neighborhood are marked as outliers (topic −1).
Step 4: Extract top words with c-TF-IDF. For each cluster, c-TF-IDF identifies the words that appear more often in that cluster than across the whole dataset. These are the distinctive words: the ones that make this group different from the others.
Step 5: Label with llama3.1. The top words and three example passages from each cluster are sent to a local LLM (llama3.1 through Ollama). The model writes a human-readable topic name and a one-sentence description. This label is a suggestion; you should always check it against the top words and examples.






TipKey terms



Embedding: a list of numbers that represents text meaning as a position in high-dimensional space. Two embeddings that are numerically close represent texts with similar meaning.
UMAP: a dimensionality reduction algorithm that compresses high-dimensional embeddings to a smaller number of dimensions while keeping similar items near each other.
HDBSCAN: a density-based clustering algorithm. It finds groups by looking for regions where points are unusually close together. It does not force a fixed number of equally-sized clusters.
c-TF-IDF: class-level TF-IDF. It finds words that are distinctive for a cluster relative to the full dataset.
Outlier topic (−1): paragraphs HDBSCAN could not assign to any dense cluster. A small number of outliers is normal and expected.

title: What Is Topic Modeling?
section: How to Read the Topic Review Table
text:
How to Read the Topic Review Table
Start with topic_review_table.csv. Open it in Excel or Google Sheets.







Column
What to look for




topic_label
The name llama3.1 suggested — treat it as a starting point


documents
How many paragraphs were assigned to this topic


top_words
The distinctive words from c-TF-IDF — the real evidence for the label


interviewees
Which speakers contributed paragraphs to this topic


example_ids
Paragraph IDs of the strongest matches


example_text
A short excerpt to help you judge whether the label fits









TipHow to check a label




Read the top words. Do they form a coherent idea, or do unrelated words appear together?
Read the example texts. Does the label describe them accurately?
Check the interviewees. If a topic draws from only one speaker, ask whether it reflects a genuine theme or that person’s distinctive vocabulary.
If the label is wrong, rewrite it based on what you actually see.

title: What Is Topic Modeling?
text:
Prepared Results

  Download topic review table
  Download LLM labels
  Download row assignments


Top Words per Topic
Each bar shows the most distinctive words for one topic. The length of each bar is the c-TF-IDF score: how distinctive that word is for this topic relative to all others. Read the words carefully; do the top words for each topic tell a coherent story, or do some seem mismatched?

The hover score is a c-TF-IDF weight. It measures how distinctive that word is for this topic relative to all others. The number has no standalone meaning; what matters is which words score highest within each topic, not the absolute value.


Topic Map
This chart places each topic as a circle in 2D space. Topics that are close together have more similar vocabularies. The size of each circle represents the number of paragraphs in that topic. Hover over each circle to see its label and top words.



Document Map
Each dot is one paragraph, positioned in 2D by the text embeddings. Dots of the same color belong to the same topic. Grey dots are outliers. Hover over any dot to read the paragraph text and see which topic it was assigned to.

title: What Is Topic Modeling?
text:
What the Results Show






ImportantReading the topic distribution



The model found 7 topics and 2 outlier paragraphs. The largest topic (15 of 50 paragraphs) covers transparency and honesty across five of the six speakers. Two smaller topics draw from only one speaker each: Topic 4 (Inclusive Representation, Linda) and Topic 5 (Responsible Data Management, Gina).
These single-speaker topics raise an interpretive question: do they reflect genuine thematic differences in what those speakers discuss, or do they reflect individual vocabulary patterns that the model grouped separately?
Topics 0, 1, and 2 are all transparency-adjacent. The model separated them, but they share significant vocabulary. This is worth examining: are these meaningfully distinct themes, or variations on the same idea that a different parameter setting might merge?

title: What Is Topic Modeling?
text:
Where Human Interpretation Takes Over
Every step in the pipeline involved a human decision:

choosing which interview questions to ask
deciding to split the transcript into paragraphs rather than sentences or whole interviews
choosing which LLM to use for labeling
deciding whether to accept, revise, or reject a generated label
deciding whether adjacent topics should be merged or kept separate
returning to specific passages for close reading

The pipeline organizes and surfaces patterns. Explaining what those patterns mean and why they matter for a research question is work that only a human reader can do.

Why Taguette?
Taguette is free, open-source, and runs entirely in your browser — nothing to install. It covers the core QDA workflow: import documents, create codes, highlight passages, and export results. It is a good starting point before moving to a full-featured tool like QualCoder or ATLAS.ti.
Open Taguette at: app.taguette.org. New to Taguette? See the getting started guide for a walkthrough of the basic workflow.






TipLocal vs. cloud



The hosted version at app.taguette.org is the fastest way to start. If you are working with sensitive data, use the local desktop version — your data stays on your computer.

title: Computational Approaches to Text Analysis
text: This workshop introduces computational tools for analyzing qualitative data. It is designed for researchers and students with no prior coding experience. title: 1 · Software QDA
text:
What Is Software-Assisted QDA?
Qualitative data analysis software gives you a structured environment for doing what qualitative researchers have always done: read closely, annotate, and organize meaning. The difference from paper and highlighters is scale and structure. With QDA software you can:

Code — assign labels to passages and retrieve all passages sharing a code
Memo — write interpretive notes attached to data or codes
Query — search across codes, documents, and annotations
Visualize — generate code co-occurrence maps and frequency charts

The analysis is still human-driven. The software does not find themes; it helps you track and retrieve the themes you identify.






TipWhen to use software-assisted QDA




Your dataset is small enough to read closely (dozens to low hundreds of documents)
Your research question requires careful attention to context, tone, and nuance
You are working collaboratively and need shared codebooks
Your data includes multimedia (audio, video, images)
You want to document your analytical process for transparency



Most QDA tools support a common set of data types:







Data type
Examples




Plain text
Interview transcripts, field notes, open-ended survey responses


Documents
PDFs, Word files


Spreadsheets
CSV exports from survey platforms


Images
Screenshots, photographs


Audio / Video
Recorded interviews, social media clips

QualCoder
QualCoder is free, open-source, and functionally comparable to commercial alternatives. It runs locally on your computer — no subscription, no cloud account, and full control over your data.

Download the demo project to explore a fully coded project before building your own.




ATLAS.ti
ATLAS.ti is one of the most widely used commercial QDA platforms. UCR Library holds a license accessible at the STAR Lab using the public account. Note that a desktop session and a web session count as two separate users.
ATLAS.ti covers the same core functions as QualCoder with a more polished interface.

ImportantAI in qualitative research: a human-first principle



AI tools can suggest codes, summarize passages, and group themes, but they cannot replace interpretive judgment. Current best practice treats the AI as a support tool, not a decision-maker:

Structure prompts incrementally, one task at a time
Review every AI suggestion before accepting it
Document your prompts, model used, and any decisions made
De-identify data before sending it to any cloud-based model
Prefer local models (Ollama) when working with sensitive transcripts

The goal is human-in-the-loop analysis, not automated coding.

title: 2 · Word Counting
text:
Data Cleaning and Pre-Processing
Before any counting happens, raw text needs to be cleaned and standardized. The choices made at this stage directly shape what the analysis surfaces.
Typical pre-processing steps:

Tokenizing: splitting the text into individual words; each word is called a token
Normalizing: converting to lowercase, removing punctuation and numbers
Filtering stop words: removing high-frequency function words that carry little meaning on their own, such as “the”, “and”, “is”
Lemmatizing: reducing words to their base form so variants count together







TipKey terms



Stop words: function words (articles, prepositions, conjunctions) that appear in nearly every document regardless of topic. Removing them lets more content-bearing words surface. The choice of stop word list affects results: “like” and “just” may need to be added manually for conversational text.
Lemmatization: grouping word variants under a shared base form. “promoting”, “promotes”, and “promoted” all become “promote”. Without lemmatization, these count separately and each appears less frequent than it actually is.

title: 2 · Word Counting
text:
What Frequency Reveals and Conceals







What frequency can show
What it misses




Which concepts recur most
Tone and evaluation (good vs. bad product)


How vocabulary differs across speakers
Sarcasm, hedging, negation


Whether certain topics cluster together
Context and sequence


Words used by only one speaker
What speakers imply but don’t say



A word that appears 15 times in one interview and once in another is worth a closer look. But frequency alone cannot tell you why it appears or what the speaker thinks about it.

title: 2 · Word Counting
text:
Voyant Tools
Voyant Tools is a browser-based text analysis environment. It requires no installation; you upload text and get immediate visualizations.
Open it at: voyant-tools.org
What Voyant provides:







Tool
What it shows




Cirrus (word cloud)
Most frequent words at a glance


Trends
How word frequency changes across documents


Summary
Top terms, document lengths, vocabulary density


Contexts
Keywords in context (KWIC): words shown in their surrounding sentences


Collocates
Words that consistently appear in the same context as a target word

title: 2 · Word Counting
text:
What Word Counting Adds
Frequency analysis works best as a starting point. It helps you:

Identify vocabulary worth tracing across speakers
Notice imbalances in who uses what language
Generate hypotheses before running more complex analyses

When you move to sentiment analysis and topic modeling, keep the frequency results in mind. Do the dominant topics match the most frequent words? Do speakers with distinctive vocabulary also cluster into distinct topics?
Full instructions: 2b · Word Counting Exercise

title: 3 · Sentiment Analysis
text:
NoteBy the end of this section you will be able to




Explain how rule-based sentiment analysis works
Interpret VADER sentiment scores applied to the interview dataset
Critically evaluate what the results reveal and what they miss

title: 3 · Sentiment Analysis
text:
What Is Sentiment Analysis?
Sentiment analysis assigns a numerical score to text to indicate whether the language is positive, negative, or neutral. It does not read for meaning; it measures the surface tone of words.
Rule-based sentiment tools work from a lexicon: a dictionary of words pre-scored for emotional valence. When the tool sees a word like honest or trust, it adds to the positive score. When it sees mislead or frustrated, it adds to the negative score. The final score is a sum of these signals, normalized to a standard scale.






TipVADER



VADER (Valence Aware Dictionary and sEntiment Reasoner) was designed for short, informal social media text. It handles:

Capitalization (GREAT scores higher than great)
Punctuation (great!!! scores higher than great)
Degree modifiers (very good > good, barely good < good)
Negation (not good flips the polarity)
Common slang and emoji

VADER returns four scores per text:







Score
Meaning




positive
Proportion of tokens with positive valence


negative
Proportion of tokens with negative valence


neutral
Proportion of neutral tokens


compound
Overall score, normalized to −1.0 (most negative) to +1.0 (most positive)



A compound score ≥ +0.05 is classified positive; ≤ −0.05 is negative; between is neutral.

title: 3 · Sentiment Analysis
text:
Results
The scores below were computed on all 50 interview paragraphs. Download the full results to explore individual scores.

  Download sentiment scores


Distribution of Compound Scores

48 of 50 paragraphs score as positive. Compound scores cluster between +0.70 and +0.98.


Scores by Interviewee

All six speakers have median compound scores above +0.75. The spread within each speaker is narrow. There is almost no variation across the dataset.

title: 3 · Sentiment Analysis
text:
Interpreting the Results






ImportantThe central interpretive question



If 48 of 50 paragraphs score as positive, what does that actually mean?
It could mean the speakers are genuinely positive. But it more likely reveals something about genre. These are interview responses in which influencers are explaining and justifying their professional practices. That genre calls for positive, confident language, even when describing a problem.
VADER was trained on tweets and product reviews, where positive/negative signals are direct and intentional. Interview responses tend to use positively valenced words (honest, trust, values, responsible) to frame what are often complex or ambiguous situations.
The tool cannot distinguish between: - “I believe in transparency” (genuine conviction) - “I always say I believe in transparency” (performative) - “I believe in transparency, but sometimes it’s difficult” (with reservation)
All three would score very similarly.



What the scores do reveal
Even within a uniformly positive distribution, variation matters:

Ben-003 is one of the only negative-scoring paragraphs. Read it: Ben is describing other influencers’ unethical behavior. The negative score tracks the critique.
Speakers with lower averages (Ben, Gina) tend to use more hedged or critical language than those at the top (Alex, Otto).
The width of the box plots for each speaker indicates how consistent their tone is across their responses.

title: 3 · Sentiment Analysis
text:
Discussion

Why might professional interview language consistently score as positive even when the content involves criticism?
Does high sentiment mean the speaker is being sincere or polished?
What kind of text would VADER analyze more reliably than these interviews?
If you used a different sentiment tool trained on formal professional speech, would you expect the results to differ? In what direction?

title: 3 · Sentiment Analysis
text:
What Sentiment Analysis Adds
Sentiment analysis is most useful when:

You have a large corpus where manual reading is impractical
The text comes from genres where sentiment is direct (social media, reviews, comment sections)
You are comparing sentiment between categories (speakers, time periods, platforms)

For interview data, the near-uniform positive result tells you something important: the genre shapes the signal. Any computational method applied to interview text will run into the same issue in some form.
As you move to topic modeling, consider whether the method reveals something that sentiment cannot, or whether it runs into the same genre constraints.

title: 4b · Topic Modeling Exercise
text:
NoteBy the end of this exercise you will have




Embeddings generated for all 50 interview paragraphs using nomic-embed-text
A set of topics labeled by llama3.1
A topic review table and four interactive visualizations
A short written interpretation of one topic
This exercise has two paths. Choose the one that fits where you are right now.
Path A: Run the pipeline. Requires Python 3.11, Ollama, and two local models. You generate your own results from scratch.
Path B: Use reference results. Skip all setup and work directly with the prepared outputs. You complete the same interpretation task.

title: 4b · Topic Modeling Exercise
text:
Step 1 — Get the Project Files
Clone the repository to your computer:
git clone https://github.com/jinghanlib/computational-approaches-text-analysis.git
cd computational-approaches-text-analysis
If you do not have git installed, download the ZIP from the repository page and unzip it.
Then open data/interviews.csv in Excel or Google Sheets. Before running anything, read 5–8 paragraphs and write down the themes you expect to see. You will compare this prediction to the model output later.

title: 4b · Topic Modeling Exercise
section: Step 2 — Install Ollama and Pull the Models (Path A only)
text:
Step 2 — Install Ollama and Pull the Models (Path A only)
The pipeline uses two local models that run through Ollama. No internet connection is required once they are downloaded.
1. Download and install Ollama. Go to ollama.com and click the download button for your operating system.
Mac: Open the downloaded .dmg file, drag Ollama to your Applications folder, then launch it from Applications. The Ollama icon will appear in the menu bar.
Windows: Run the downloaded .exe installer and follow the prompts. Ollama will start automatically and appear as an icon in the system tray (bottom right of the taskbar). If it does not start automatically, search for “Ollama” in the Start menu and open it.
2. Open a terminal and pull the models. Once Ollama is running, open a terminal. Location does not matter for this step.
Mac: Open the Terminal app from Applications → Utilities → Terminal.
Windows: Press Windows key + R, type cmd, and press Enter to open Command Prompt. Alternatively, search for “PowerShell” in the Start menu and open it.
Then run these two commands, one at a time. Wait for each to finish before running the next:
ollama pull nomic-embed-text
ollama pull llama3.1
Each command downloads the model and saves it locally to your computer.






TipDownload sizes




nomic-embed-text: ~300 MB (required)
llama3.1: ~5 GB (used to generate topic labels; optional if storage is tight — see Step 4 for how to run without it)

You only need to pull the models once. They stay on your computer for future use.


3. Confirm Ollama is running before moving to the next step. On Mac, look for the Ollama icon in the menu bar. On Windows, check the system tray at the bottom right of the screen.

title: 4b · Topic Modeling Exercise
section: Step 3 — Set Up Python (Path A only)
text:
Step 3 — Set Up Python (Path A only)
Open a terminal directly inside the project folder computational-approaches-text-analysis.
Mac: In Finder, navigate into the folder. Right-click (or Control-click) on it and choose New Terminal at Folder. If that option is not visible, go to System Settings → Keyboard → Keyboard Shortcuts → Services and enable “New Terminal at Folder”.
Windows: In File Explorer, navigate into the folder. Click on the address bar at the top, type powershell, and press Enter. A PowerShell window will open already inside the folder.
You can verify you are in the right place by running ls (Mac) or dir (Windows). You should see folders named data, scripts, and outputs.
Create and activate a virtual environment, then install the required packages.
Mac:
python3.11 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python3.11 -m pip install -r requirements.txt
Windows:
python3.11 -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
python3.11 -m pip install -r requirements.txt
This installs bertopic, umap-learn, hdbscan, pandas, plotly, and requests.

title: 4b · Topic Modeling Exercise
text:
Step 4 — Run the Pipeline
In the same terminal from Step 3 (with the virtual environment still active), run the script with a custom output directory so your results do not overwrite the prepared reference files:
python3.11 scripts/run_bertopic.py --output-dir outputs/my_run
The script will print its progress as it works through each stage:
Loaded 50 paragraphs from data/interviews.csv
Embedding 50 paragraphs with nomic-embed-text …
  Embedded 10/50
  …
Running BERTopic …
Found 7 topics, 2 outlier paragraphs (topic -1)
Labeling topics with llama3.1:latest …
  Topic 0: Importance of Transparency and Honesty in Digital Influencing
  …
Saving visualizations …
Results written to outputs/my_run






TipEmbeddings are cached



The first run embeds all 50 paragraphs, which takes a few minutes. On any later run, the cached .npy file is reused automatically, so re-runs are much faster.








WarningIf you do not have llama3.1 (5 GB)



Skip the labeling step. The script will fall back to c-TF-IDF names:
python3.11 scripts/run_bertopic.py --output-dir outputs/my_run --skip-labels

title: 4b · Topic Modeling Exercise
text:
Step 6 — Interpret One Topic
Open topic_review_table.csv and choose one topic to focus on. Answer these questions:

What is the topic label (from llama3.1)?
Which top words support the label? Which seem mismatched or vague?
Which example text best represents the topic? Quote a phrase.
Which interviewees contributed paragraphs to this topic? Does that distribution surprise you?
Would you keep the label, revise it, or split it into two separate ideas?
What would you need to read closely before making a research claim?

title: 4b · Topic Modeling Exercise
text:
Step 7 — Discussion
The model found 7 topics. Topics 0, 1, and 2 are all transparency-adjacent. Topics 4 and 5 each draw from only one speaker.
Discuss:

Topics 0, 1, and 2 share similar vocabulary. Are these meaningfully distinct themes, or does the model separate them based on surface differences? What would you need to read to decide?
Topic 4 (Inclusive Representation) comes entirely from Linda. Topic 5 (Responsible Data Management) comes entirely from Gina. Does this reflect a genuine thematic difference, or individual vocabulary?
In the document map, look at how the topic clusters are positioned. Are any scattered across the space or tightly packed? What does the spatial spread suggest about their coherence?
How would the topic distribution look if the dataset included speakers with opposing views on disclosure norms?

title: 4b · Topic Modeling Exercise
section: Step 8 — Compare Your Prediction with the Model
text:
Step 8 — Compare Your Prediction with the Model
You wrote down expected themes in Step 1. Compare:

Which topic matched your prediction?
Which topic surprised you?
Did the model capture meaning, or just repeated vocabulary?

title: 4b · Topic Modeling Exercise
text:
Step 9 — Write 120–180 Words
Use this template:

The topic model found that one recurring theme in these interviews is _____. I know this because the top words include _____ and the example passage says _____. The model identified 7 topics; two of them draw from only one speaker. This likely reflects _____. However, I would be careful about claiming _____ because _____. A researcher following up should read _____ closely and also consider whether adjacent topics should be merged or treated as distinct.

title: 4b · Topic Modeling Exercise
text:
Common Problems
Ollama is not running. Start Ollama from the Applications folder (Mac) or run ollama serve in a terminal. The Ollama icon should appear in the menu bar before you run the script.
nomic-embed-text model not found. Run ollama pull nomic-embed-text and wait for the download to complete.
python3.11 is not recognized. Check which Python versions are installed: python3 --version. If python3 is version 3.11, replace python3.11 with python3.
Wrong folder. Your terminal must be in the project folder — the one that contains data/, scripts/, outputs/, and requirements.txt.
